questions.stem: Calculate the area of the rectangle shown in the diagram.
questions.hint: Area of a rectangle = length \(\times\) width.
questions.solution: Area = \(6 \times 4 = 24\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Identify the shape and the two given dimensions from the diagram: a rectangle with length \(6\text{ cm}\) and width \(4\text{ cm}\).
Recall the area formula for a rectangle. Area is the product of the two perpendicular side lengths.
Substitute the known values into the formula.
Multiply carefully and include the square unit. Check that the result matches one of the options.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the parallelogram shown in the diagram.
questions.hint: Area of a parallelogram = base \(\times\) perpendicular height (not a slanted side).
questions.solution: Area = \(6 \times 8 = 48\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: From the diagram, the base is \(6\text{ cm}\) and the perpendicular height is the dashed altitude of \(8\text{ cm}\). Do not use a slanted side as the height.
The area of a parallelogram is base times perpendicular height — the same idea as a rectangle after “pushing” the slanted sides upright.
Substitute the values.
Evaluate and write the answer with square centimetres.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the triangle shown in the diagram.
questions.hint: Area of a triangle = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times\) base \(\times\) height.
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 6 = 24\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Read the base and the perpendicular height from the diagram. The height meets the base at right angles.
A triangle is half of a parallelogram (or rectangle) with the same base and height, so the formula includes the factor \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).
Substitute and multiply base by height first.
Halve to finish, and attach the correct unit.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the obtuse-angled triangle shown in the diagram.
questions.hint: Even when the height falls outside the triangle, area is still \(\dfrac{1}{2}bh\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 5 = 15\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: The triangle is obtuse, so the perpendicular height from the opposite vertex lands outside the base. The diagram still labels base \(6\text{ cm}\) and height \(5\text{ cm}\).
The area formula does not change for obtuse triangles — still half base times perpendicular height.
Substitute the values.
Simplify to the final area.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the trapezium shown in the diagram.
questions.hint: Area of a trapezium = \(\dfrac{1}{2}(a + b)h\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are the parallel sides.
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2}(5 + 9) \times 4 = 28\text{ m}^2\).

steps.explain: A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides. Here those lengths are \(a = 5\text{ m}\) and \(b = 9\text{ m}\), with perpendicular height \(h = 4\text{ m}\).
Use the trapezium area formula: average the two parallel sides, then multiply by the height.
Add the parallel sides, then multiply by the height.
Compute \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 14 = 7\), then \(7 \times 4 = 28\).

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the right-angled trapezium shown in the diagram.
questions.hint: Right angles mark the perpendicular height. Still use \(\dfrac{1}{2}(a + b)h\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2}(6 + 8) \times 5 = 35\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: The right angles show that the vertical side is the perpendicular height \(h = 5\text{ cm}\). The two parallel sides are \(6\text{ cm}\) and \(8\text{ cm}\).
Apply the trapezium formula.
Substitute and simplify the sum of the parallel sides.
Evaluate: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 14 = 7\), then \(7 \times 5 = 35\).

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the circle with radius \(5\text{ cm}\). Give the answer in exact form and correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Area of a circle = \(\pi r^2\). Square the radius, then multiply by \(\pi\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\pi \times 5^2 = 25\pi\text{ cm}^2 \approx 78.54\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: The radius is given as \(r = 5\text{ cm}\).
Use the circle area formula \(A = \pi r^2\).
Square the radius: \(5^2 = 25\). The exact area is therefore \(25\pi\).
For a two-decimal approximation use \(\pi \approx 3.1416\): \(25 \times 3.1416 \approx 78.54\).

questions.stem: Calculate the area of a circle with a diameter of \(10\text{ cm}\). Give the answer in exact form and correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: First find the radius: \(r = d/2\). Then use \(A = \pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Radius \(r = 5\text{ cm}\). Area = \(25\pi\text{ cm}^2 \approx 78.54\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: The diameter is \(10\text{ cm}\). Radius is half the diameter.
Write the circle area formula.
Substitute \(r = 5\) to get the exact area.
Approximate: \(25\pi \approx 78.54\text{ cm}^2\) (2 d.p.).

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the right-angled trapezium shown in the diagram.
questions.hint: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2}(a + b)h\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 6) \times 4 = 18\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Parallel sides are \(3\text{ cm}\) and \(6\text{ cm}\); the perpendicular height is \(4\text{ cm}\).
Use the trapezium area formula.
Add the parallel sides, then multiply by height.
Simplify: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 9 = 4.5\), then \(4.5 \times 4 = 18\).

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the parallelogram shown in the diagram.
questions.hint: Area = base \(\times\) height.
questions.solution: Area = \(5 \times 3 = 15\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Base \(b = 5\text{ cm}\) and perpendicular height \(h = 3\text{ cm}\) are marked on the diagram.
Parallelogram area formula: product of base and perpendicular height.
Substitute.
Multiply to obtain the area.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the rhombus with diagonals of length \(8\text{ cm}\) and \(6\text{ cm}\).
questions.hint: Area of a rhombus = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times d_1 \times d_2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 6 = 24\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: A rhombus has perpendicular diagonals. Here \(d_1 = 8\text{ cm}\) and \(d_2 = 6\text{ cm}\).
The area formula using diagonals is half their product (the diagonals split the rhombus into four right triangles).
Substitute the diagonal lengths.
Halve to finish.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the kite with diagonals of length \(18\text{ cm}\) and \(14\text{ cm}\).
questions.hint: Area of a kite = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times d_1 \times d_2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 14 = 126\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: The diagonals of a kite are perpendicular. Given lengths: \(18\text{ cm}\) and \(14\text{ cm}\).
Use the diagonal formula for a kite.
Multiply the diagonals: \(18 \times 14 = 252\).
Halve \(252\) to get the area.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the kite with diagonals of length \(4\text{ m}\) and \(16\text{ m}\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 16 = 32\text{ m}^2\).

steps.explain: Diagonals: \(d_1 = 4\text{ m}\), \(d_2 = 16\text{ m}\).
Kite area formula with diagonals.
Substitute.
Simplify.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the rhombus with diagonals of length \(16\text{ mm}\) and \(24\text{ mm}\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 24 = 192\text{ mm}^2\).

steps.explain: Diagonals of the rhombus: \(16\text{ mm}\) and \(24\text{ mm}\).
Apply \(A = \tfrac{1}{2}d_1 d_2\).
Compute half of 16 first to simplify: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 16 = 8\).
Multiply: \(8 \times 24 = 192\).

questions.stem: Find the area of a rectangle with side lengths \(4\text{ m}\) and \(7\text{ m}\).
questions.hint: Area = length \(\times\) width.
questions.solution: Area = \(4 \times 7 = 28\text{ m}^2\).

steps.explain: A rectangle has sides \(4\text{ m}\) and \(7\text{ m}\).
Area formula for a rectangle.
Substitute.
Multiply.

questions.stem: Find the area of a square with side length \(8\text{ cm}\).
questions.hint: Area of a square = side\(^2\).

steps.explain: A square has all sides equal; each side is \(8\text{ cm}\).
Area of a square is the side length squared.
Square 8.
Include the square unit.

questions.stem: Find the area of a circle with a diameter of \(10\text{ m}\). Give the answer in exact form.
questions.hint: First find \(r = d/2\), then \(A = \pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Radius \(r = 5\text{ m}\). Area = \(25\pi\text{ m}^2\).

steps.explain: Diameter is \(10\text{ m}\), so the radius is half of that.
Circle area formula.
Substitute \(r = 5\).
Leave the answer in exact form with the correct unit.

questions.stem: Find the area of a rhombus with diagonals \(8\text{ cm}\) and \(5\text{ cm}\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 5 = 20\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Diagonals: \(8\text{ cm}\) and \(5\text{ cm}\).
Rhombus area using diagonals.
Substitute.
Multiply.

questions.stem: Find the area of a kite with diagonals \(4\text{ m}\) and \(3\text{ m}\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3 = 6\text{ m}^2\).

steps.explain: Diagonals of the kite are \(4\text{ m}\) and \(3\text{ m}\).
Use the kite diagonal formula.
Substitute.
Simplify.

questions.stem: Find the area of a square with a diagonal of length \(8\text{ cm}\).
questions.hint: A square is a rhombus with equal diagonals: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}d^2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 8^2 = 32\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: In a square both diagonals are equal and perpendicular, each of length \(d = 8\text{ cm}\).
Treat the square as a rhombus and use the diagonal area formula.
Square the diagonal: \(8^2 = 64\).
Halve to obtain the area of the square.

questions.stem: A trapezium has parallel sides of lengths \(b_1\) and \(b_2\) and perpendicular height \(h\). By placing a second identical copy upside down next to the first, a parallelogram is formed. What is the correct derivation of the trapezium area formula?
options: \(A = (b_1 + b_2)h\) because the parallelogram has base \(b_1 + b_2\) and height \(h\)
\(A = b_1 b_2 h\) by multiplying all three given lengths
\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h\), since the parallelogram of area \((b_1 + b_2)h\) is made of two identical trapeziums
\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}b_1 b_2\), treating the parallel sides like diagonals of a kite
questions.hint: Two copies make a parallelogram of base \(b_1 + b_2\) and height \(h\); one trapezium is half of that.
questions.solution: Two copies form a parallelogram of area \((b_1 + b_2)h\). One trapezium is half: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h\).

steps.explain: Start with trapezium \(ABCD\) having parallel sides \(b_1\) and \(b_2\) and height \(h\). Make a second identical copy and rotate it \(180^\circ\) so the two non-parallel sides join.
The combined figure is a parallelogram whose base is the sum of the two parallel sides and whose height is still \(h\).
The parallelogram is made of two identical trapeziums, so each has half the parallelogram’s area.
This is the standard trapezium formula. Choose the option that states both the parallelogram area and the final half-factor.

questions.stem: A kite has perpendicular diagonals of lengths \(d_1\) and \(d_2\). It is enclosed in a rectangle of dimensions \(d_1 \times d_2\). Which statement correctly derives the kite’s area?
options: \(A = d_1 d_2\) because the kite fills the whole rectangle
\(A = 2d_1 d_2\) because four triangles make two rectangles
\(A = \dfrac{1}{4}d_1 d_2\) because only one of the four right triangles is shaded
\(A = \dfrac{1}{2}d_1 d_2\) because the kite occupies exactly half of the enclosing rectangle
questions.hint: The kite’s four right triangles match the four corner triangles left outside it — so the kite is half the rectangle.
questions.solution: Rectangle area = \(d_1 d_2\). The kite is half of that rectangle: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}d_1 d_2\).

steps.explain: Enclose the kite in a rectangle whose sides are parallel to the diagonals, so the rectangle measures \(d_1\) by \(d_2\).
The diagonals divide the rectangle into four smaller rectangles, each split by a kite side into two congruent right triangles — one inside the kite and one outside.
Therefore the kite’s area equals the total of the outer corner regions, which is half the rectangle.
Substitute the rectangle area to obtain the standard formula.

questions.stem: Find the area of the circle with radius \(6\text{ cm}\). Give the answer in exact form.
questions.hint: Area = \(\pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\pi \times 6^2 = 36\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Radius is \(r = 6\text{ cm}\).
Circle area formula.
Square the radius: \(6^2 = 36\).
Write the exact area.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the semicircle with radius \(8\text{ cm}\). Give the answer in exact form.
questions.hint: Semicircle area = half of \(\pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi \times 8^2 = 32\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: A semicircle is half a full circle of the same radius \(r = 8\text{ cm}\).
Full circle area would be \(\pi r^2\); take half of that.
Compute \(r^2 = 64\), so full circle is \(64\pi\).
Halve to get the semicircle area.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the quadrant (quarter circle) with radius \(12\text{ cm}\). Give the answer in exact form.
questions.hint: Quadrant area = one quarter of \(\pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi \times 12^2 = 36\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: A quadrant is one quarter of a full circle with radius \(r = 12\text{ cm}\).
Write the quadrant formula.
Square the radius: \(12^2 = 144\). Full circle area is \(144\pi\).
Divide by 4.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the sector with radius \(9\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(120^\circ\). Give the answer in exact form.
questions.hint: Sector area = \(\dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{120}{360}\pi \times 9^2 = 27\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Sector of radius \(r = 9\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(\theta = 120^\circ\).
A sector is the fraction \(\theta/360\) of the full circle area \(\pi r^2\).
Simplify the fraction: \(\dfrac{120}{360} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Also \(r^2 = 81\).
Compute \(\dfrac{81}{3} = 27\).

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the major sector with radius \(8\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(270^\circ\). Give the answer in exact form.
questions.hint: Major sector still uses \(\dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2\) with \(\theta = 270^\circ\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{270}{360}\pi \times 8^2 = 48\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Major sector: radius \(8\text{ cm}\), central angle \(270^\circ\) (three-quarters of a full turn).
Use the sector formula with the given angle (already the major angle).
Compute \(\dfrac{3}{4} \times 64 = 48\).

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the sector with radius \(12\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(30^\circ\). Give the answer in exact form.
questions.hint: Sector area = \(\dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{30}{360}\pi \times 12^2 = 12\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Radius \(r = 12\text{ cm}\), angle \(\theta = 30^\circ\).
Sector formula.
Simplify fraction: \(\dfrac{30}{360} = \dfrac{1}{12}\). Also \(r^2 = 144\).
Compute \(\dfrac{144}{12} = 12\).

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the sector with radius \(8\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(45^\circ\). Give the answer in exact form.
questions.hint: Sector area = \(\dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Area = \(\dfrac{45}{360}\pi \times 8^2 = 8\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Radius \(r = 8\text{ cm}\), angle \(\theta = 45^\circ\).
Sector formula.
Simplify: \(\dfrac{45}{360} = \dfrac{1}{8}\) and \(r^2 = 64\).
Compute \(\dfrac{64}{8} = 8\).

questions.stem: Choose the correct algebraic expression for the area \(A\) of a sector with radius \(r\) and central angle \(\theta^\circ\).
questions.hint: A sector is the fraction \(\theta/360\) of the full circle area \(\pi r^2\).
questions.solution: Full circle area is \(\pi r^2\). Fraction of the circle is \(\dfrac{\theta}{360}\), so \(A = \dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2\).

steps.explain: A full circle corresponds to a central angle of \(360^\circ\) and has area \(\pi r^2\).
A sector with central angle \(\theta^\circ\) is the fraction \(\dfrac{\theta}{360}\) of the full circle.
Multiply the full-circle area by that fraction. Do not use circumference \(2\pi r\) — that would give arc length, not area.
The correct formula is therefore \(A = \dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2\).

questions.stem: Calculate the radius of the circle with an area of \(15\text{ mm}^2\). Correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Rearrange \(A = \pi r^2\) to get \(r = \sqrt{A/\pi}\).
questions.solution: \(r = \sqrt{15/\pi} \approx 2.19\text{ mm}\).

steps.explain: Start from the area formula with \(A = 15\text{ mm}^2\).
Divide both sides by \(\pi\) to isolate \(r^2\).
Take the positive square root (length cannot be negative).
Evaluate and round to two decimal places.

questions.stem: Calculate the radius of the circle with an area of \(80\text{ cm}^2\). Correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Use \(r = \sqrt{A/\pi}\).
questions.solution: \(r = \sqrt{80/\pi} \approx 5.05\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: Given area \(A = 80\text{ cm}^2\).
Solve for \(r^2\).
Take the square root.
Round to two decimal places. (Note: \(10.09\) would be the diameter, not the radius.)

questions.stem: Calculate the radius of a circle with an area of \(16\pi\text{ m}^2\).
questions.hint: Cancel \(\pi\) from both sides of \(\pi r^2 = 16\pi\).
questions.solution: \(\pi r^2 = 16\pi \Rightarrow r^2 = 16 \Rightarrow r = 4\text{ m}\).

steps.explain: Write the equation with the given exact area.
Divide both sides by \(\pi\) (since \(\pi \neq 0\)).
Take the positive square root.
State the radius with its unit.

questions.stem: Calculate the radius of a circle with an area of \(36\pi\text{ cm}^2\).
questions.hint: From \(\pi r^2 = 36\pi\), cancel \(\pi\) and take the square root.
questions.solution: \(r^2 = 36 \Rightarrow r = 6\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: Set up the area equation.
Cancel \(\pi\) from both sides.
Take the positive square root.
Include the unit. (\(12\text{ cm}\) would be the diameter.)

questions.stem: Find the area of the shaded ring (annulus) with an inner radius of \(4\text{ cm}\) and an outer radius of \(6\text{ cm}\). Give the answer in exact form and correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Annulus area = outer circle − inner circle = \(\pi(R^2 - r^2)\).

steps.explain: An annulus is the region between two concentric circles. Outer radius \(R = 6\text{ cm}\), inner radius \(r = 4\text{ cm}\).
Subtract the inner area from the outer area: \(A = \pi R^2 - \pi r^2 = \pi(R^2 - r^2)\).
Compute the difference of squares: \(6^2 - 4^2 = 36 - 16 = 20\).
Approximate: \(20\pi \approx 62.83\text{ cm}^2\) (2 d.p.).

questions.stem: Calculate the radius of a circle whose area is half that of a circle with a radius of \(8\text{ cm}\). Correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Halving the area multiplies the radius by \(\sqrt{1/2}\), not by \(1/2\).
questions.solution: Larger area \(64\pi\). Half is \(32\pi\). \(r = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: Area of the larger circle with radius 8 cm.
The smaller circle has half that area.
Solve \(\pi r^2 = 32\pi\) for \(r\).
Decimal approximation: \(4\sqrt{2} \approx 5.66\text{ cm}\). (Halving the radius would wrongly give area one quarter.)

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the composite L-shaped region with the following dimensions:
questions.hint: Split the L into two rectangles.
questions.solution: Left rectangle \(6 \times 10 = 60\). Right rectangle \(6 \times 6 = 36\). Total \(96\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Split the L-shape into a tall left rectangle and a shorter right rectangle. Left width equals the top side: \(6\text{ cm}\); left height is the full \(10\text{ cm}\).
Right rectangle width is the remaining base: \(12 - 6 = 6\text{ cm}\). Its height is \(10 - 4 = 6\text{ cm}\).
Add the two rectangular areas.
Total area of the L-shape.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the composite U-shaped region with the following dimensions:
questions.hint: Outer rectangle minus the inner rectangular cutout.
questions.solution: Outer \(18 \times 15 = 270\). Cutout \(10 \times 10 = 100\). Area \(170\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Compute the area of the outer bounding rectangle.
Inner cutout width = total width minus both legs: \(18 - 4 - 4 = 10\text{ cm}\). Cutout height is given as \(10\text{ cm}\).
Subtract the cutout from the outer rectangle.
U-shaped region area.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the house-shaped composite region consisting of a rectangle and a triangular roof with:
questions.hint: Rectangle + triangle. Triangle height = \(7 - 4 = 3\).
questions.solution: Rectangle \(24\). Triangle \(9\). Total \(33\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Split into a rectangle of base 6 cm and height 4 cm, plus a triangular roof.
Roof triangle has the same base 6 cm. Its height is total height minus rectangle height: \(7 - 4 = 3\text{ cm}\).
Add the two parts.
Total house-shaped area.

Calculate the area of the composite shape consisting of a rectangle with a semicircle on top of it:


Round the final answer to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Semicircle diameter equals the rectangle width 6 cm, so radius is 3 cm.
questions.solution: Rectangle 18 + semicircle \(4.5\pi \approx 14.14\) → total \(\approx 32.14\text{ cm}^2\).

Semicircle sits on the width 6 cm, so diameter is 6 cm and radius is 3 cm.
Semicircle area = half of \(\pi r^2\).
Add both parts and round to 2 d.p.

Calculate the area of a stadium track made from a central rectangle and two semicircles at each end:

Round the final answer to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Two semicircles make one full circle of diameter 10 m. Add that to the rectangle.
questions.solution: Rectangle 150 + circle \(25\pi \approx 78.54\) → total \(\approx 228.54\text{ m}^2\).

steps.explain: Central rectangle: length 15 m, width 10 m.
The two end semicircles together make one full circle whose diameter equals the rectangle width 10 m, so radius is 5 m.
Full circle area.
Add rectangle and circle. Do not stop at 150 — that ignores the rounded ends.

questions.stem:
Calculate the area of the composite shape consisting of a rectangle on the left and a quadrant (quarter circle) on the right, with:
Round to two decimal places if needed.
questions.hint: Add rectangle area \(5 \times 7\) and quadrant area \(\tfrac{1}{4}\pi 5^2\).
questions.solution: Rectangle 35 + quadrant \(6.25\pi \approx 19.63\) → total \(\approx 54.63\text{ m}^2\).

Quadrant has radius equal to the rectangle width: \(r = 5\text{ m}\).
Approximate the quadrant: \(6.25\pi \approx 19.63\text{ m}^2\).
Add both parts. Stopping at 35 would ignore the quarter circle.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the composite step-like shape with the following dimensions:
questions.hint: Split into two rectangles: \(12 \times 12\) and \(12 \times 10\).
questions.solution: Left 144 + right 120 = 264 cm².

steps.explain: Split at the vertical step into left and right rectangles, each of width 12 cm.
Left rectangle area (full height 12 cm).
Right rectangle height is \(12 - 2 = 10\text{ cm}\).
Add the two sections.

questions.stem:
Calculate the area of the composite shape consisting of a central rectangle, a top semicircle, and a bottom triangle:

Round to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Add rectangle + semicircle (r = 5) + triangle (base 14, height 5).

steps.explain: Rectangle area.
Semicircle has diameter 10 cm, so radius 5 cm. Area is half of \(\pi r^2\).
Bottom triangle: base 14 cm, height 5 cm.
Sum all three parts and round to 2 d.p.

questions.stem: Calculate the perimeter of a sector with radius \(r = 24\) cm and angle \(\theta = 280°\) correct to 2 decimal places.

steps.explain: The perimeter of a sector consists of the arc length plus two radii.
Calculate the arc length using the formula: arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr
Evaluate numerically.
Add the two radii to get the perimeter.

questions.stem: Find the radius of a sector with angle \(\theta = 120°\) and area \(A = 75\) cm² correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution: From A = (θ/360°) × πr², we get 75 = (1/3) × πr², so r² = 225/π ≈ 71.62, r ≈ 8.5 cm

steps.explain: Use the formula for the area of a sector: A = (θ/360°) × πr²
Substitute the known values: A = 75 cm² and θ = 120°
Solve for r².
Take the square root.

questions.stem: Find the Surface Area of the following, leaving your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.hint: The surface area of a rectangular prism is \(2(lw + lh + wh)\).

steps.explain: Identify the dimensions of the rectangular prism.
Use the surface area formula \(SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)\).
Calculate the area of each pair of faces.
Add them together.

questions.stem: Find the Surface Area of the following square-based pyramid, leaving your answer to the nearest whole number. The base is a square of side 4 m, and the perpendicular vertical height is 6 m.
questions.hint: First find the slant height of the triangular faces using Pythagoras theorem. Then calculate the area of the square base and the 4 triangular faces.

steps.explain: The base is a square with side length 4 m. The area of the base is:
To find the area of the triangular faces, we need the slant height (\(s\)). Consider the right-angled triangle formed by the vertical height (6 m), half the base width (2 m), and the slant height.
Calculate the slant height.

The area of a sector is the fraction $\frac{\theta}{360}$ of the full circle’s area $\pi r^2$.
Substitute the known area $A=75$ and angle $\theta=120^\circ$.
Simplify the fraction $\frac{120}{360}$ to $\frac{1}{3}$.
Multiply both sides by $3$, then divide both sides by $\pi$ to isolate $r^2$.
Take the square root of both sides and round to 1 decimal place.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a rectangular prism of clay with \(AB=20\text{ cm}\), \(BC=16\text{ cm}\), \(EA=40\text{ cm}\). A corner has been sliced off through the planar rectangular cut \(PQRS\), where \(EP=HQ=15\text{ cm}\) and \(SB=RC=30\text{ cm}\) (so \(AP=25\text{ cm}\) and \(BS=30\text{ cm}\) remain on the two front vertical edges). Calculate the exact surface area of the prism that remains.
questions.hint: The remaining solid is a trapezoidal prism. Find each of its 6 faces separately: the base, the two trapezoidal ends (front and back), the two side rectangles, and the slanted cut face \(PQRS\) (use Pythagoras for its slant width).

steps.explain: Find the bottom face \(ABCD\), an unchanged \(20\times16\) rectangle.
Find the front and back trapezoidal faces (\(ABSP\) and \(DCRQ\)), each with parallel sides \(AP=25\) and \(BS=30\), and width \(20\).
Find the two side rectangles: the left face \(ADQP\) (\(16\times25\)) and the right face \(BCRS\) (\(16\times30\)).
Find the slanted cut face \(PQRS\): one side is \(PQ=16\) (same as \(BC\)); the other side \(PS\) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs \(20\) (horizontal) and \(30-25=5\) (vertical rise).
Add all six faces together for the total surface area.

questions.hint: The curved surface area is half of the curved surface area of a full cylinder: CSA = \pi r h.
questions.solution:
The curved surface area of a half-cylinder is half of the curved surface of a full cylinder:
\[\text{CSA} = \frac{1}{2} \times 2\pi r h = \pi r h\]
Substitute \(r = 4\) and \(h = 20\):
\[\text{CSA} = \pi \times 4 \times 20 = 80\pi\text{ cm}^2\]

\[80\pi \approx 251.327\text{ cm}^2 \implies 251.33\text{ cm}^2\]

steps.work:

A half-cylinder curved surface area is half of that:

questions.stem:
A cylinder of radius \(2\\text{ cm}\) and height \(5\\text{ cm}\) is mounted on a larger cylinder of radius \(5\\text{ cm}\) and height \(4\\text{ cm}\). Find the area of the visible surfaces, if the larger cylinder is sitting on a table.
(Round the final answer to two decimal places.)
questions.hint: Sum the curved surface of both cylinders, the top of the smaller cylinder, and the top ring area of the larger cylinder.
questions.solution:
The visible surfaces consist of:
1. Curved surface of top cylinder: \(2\pi r_1 h_1 = 2\pi(2)(5) = 20\pi\text{ cm}^2\)
2. Top circle of top cylinder: \(\pi r_1^2 = \pi(2)^2 = 4\pi\text{ cm}^2\)
3. Curved surface of bottom cylinder: \(2\pi r_2 h_2 = 2\pi(5)(4) = 40\text{ cm}^2\)
4. Exposed top ring of bottom cylinder: \(\pi r_2^2 - \pi r_1^2 = 25\pi - 4\pi = 21\pi\text{ cm}^2\)

Add the components to find the total visible area:
\[\text{SA} = 20\pi + 4\pi + 40\pi + 21\pi = 85\pi\text{ cm}^2\]
Evaluate the numerical value:
\[85\pi \approx 267.035\text{ cm}^2 \implies 267.04\text{ cm}^2\]

steps.explain: Identify all visible surfaces when sitting on a table.
steps.work:
Visible Area = (Curved surface of small cylinder) + (Curved surface of large cylinder) + (Top of small cylinder) + (Exposed top ring of large cylinder).
The bottom of the large cylinder is hidden by the table.

steps.explain: Calculate the curved surface areas (CSA = \(2\pi rh\)).
Calculate the top flat surfaces.
steps.work:
Small top = \(\pi (2)^2 = 4\pi\)
Exposed large top ring = (Area of large circle) - (Area of small circle)
Ring = \(\pi (5)^2 - \pi (2)^2 = 25\pi - 4\pi = 21\pi\)

steps.explain: Add them all together.

questions.stem: The total surface area of a cylinder is \(37.70\\text{ m}^2\) and the radius of the base is \(1.5\\text{ m}\). Find the height of the cylinder, correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Set up the equation using SA = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h and solve for h.
questions.solution:
Use the surface area formula:
\[\text{SA} = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h\]
Substitute the given values, noting that \(37.70 \approx 12\pi\):
\[12\pi = 2\pi(1.5)^2 + 2\pi(1.5)h\]
\[12\pi = 4.5\pi + 3\pi h\]
Subtract \(4.5\pi\) from both sides:
\[7.5\pi = 3\pi h\]
Divide by \(3\pi\):
\[h = \frac{7.5}{3} = 2.5\text{ m}\]

steps.explain: Set up the total surface area formula.
Substitute the given values (\(r = 1.5\), \(TSA = 37.70\)).
Rearrange and solve for \(h\).

questions.stem: The radius of a cylinder is equal to its height, and it has a total surface area of \(400\\text{ cm}^2\). Find its height, correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Since r = h, substitute r with h in the formula: SA = 2\pi h^2 + 2\pi h^2 = 4\pi h^2.
questions.solution:
Given \(r = h\), substitute \(r = h\) into the surface area formula:
\[\text{SA} = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h = 2\pi h^2 + 2\pi h^2 = 4\pi h^2\]
Set \(4\pi h^2 = 400\):
\[h^2 = \frac{400}{4\pi} = \frac{100}{\pi}\]
\[h = \sqrt{\frac{100}{\pi}} \approx 5.6419\text{ cm} \implies 5.64\text{ cm}\]

steps.explain: Set up the total surface area formula.
Substitute \(r = h\) into the equation.
Rearrange and solve for \(h\).

questions.stem: The height of a cylinder is equal to its diameter, and it has a total surface area of \(600\\text{ cm}^2\). Find the radius, correct to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Since height is diameter (h = 2r), substitute h with 2r in the formula: SA = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r(2r) = 6\pi r^2.
questions.solution:
Given \(h = 2r\), substitute \(h = 2r\) into the surface area formula:
\[\text{SA} = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r(2r) = 2\pi r^2 + 4\pi r^2 = 6\pi r^2\]
Set \(6\pi r^2 = 600\):
\[r^2 = \frac{600}{6\pi} = \frac{100}{\pi}\]
\[r = \sqrt{\frac{100}{\pi}} \approx 5.6419\text{ cm} \implies 5.64\text{ cm}\]

steps.explain: Express height in terms of radius.
steps.work: The height equals the diameter, so \(h = 2r\).

steps.explain: Set up the total surface area formula.
Substitute \(h = 2r\) and the TSA.
Rearrange and solve for \(r\).

questions.stem:
A \(270^{\\circ}\) sector block of cheese is cut from a cylindrical block of cheese. The original cylindrical block had:
- Radius = \(8\\text{ cm}\)
- Height = \(4\\text{ cm}\)
Find the total surface area of the remaining piece of cheese. (Round the final answer to two decimal places.)
questions.hint: The surface area includes the top and bottom sector faces (each 270/360 of a circle), the curved outer sector face, and two flat rectangular cut faces.
questions.solution:
The surface area consists of:
1. Top and bottom sector faces: \(2 \times \left(\frac{270}{360} \times \pi \times 8^2\right) = 96\pi\text{ cm}^2\)
2. Outer curved surface sector face: \(\frac{270}{360} \times 2\pi r h = \frac{3}{4} \times 2\pi(8)(4) = 48\pi\text{ cm}^2\)
3. Two flat rectangular cut faces: \(2 \times (r \times h) = 2 \times (8 \times 4) = 64\text{ cm}^2\)

Add the components to find the total surface area:
\[\text{SA} = 96\pi + 48\pi + 64 = 144\pi + 64\text{ cm}^2\]
Evaluate the numerical value:
\[144\pi + 64 \approx 452.389 + 64 = 516.389\text{ cm}^2 \implies 516.39\text{ cm}^2\]

steps.explain: Identify all the surfaces of the cheese block.
steps.work:
It is a \(270^\circ\) sector, which is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of a full cylinder. Therefore:
- Area of top + bottom = \(\frac{3}{4}\) of two full circles.
- Curved surface = \(\frac{3}{4}\) of a full cylinder curved surface.
- Plus two new flat rectangular side faces exposed by the cut.

steps.explain: Calculate the area of the curved and flat cylindrical surfaces.
steps.work:
Top + Bottom Area = \(\frac{3}{4} \times 2\pi r^2 = \frac{3}{4} \times 2\pi (8)^2 = 96\pi\)
Curved Surface Area = \(\frac{3}{4} \times 2\pi rh = \frac{3}{4} \times 2\pi (8)(4) = 48\pi\)

steps.explain: Calculate the area of the two flat rectangular sides.
steps.work:
Each rectangular side has dimensions \(r \times h\) = \(8 \times 4 = 32\).
Two rectangular sides = \(32 \times 2 = 64\).

steps.explain: Add them all together.

The volume of any prism equals the area of its (constant) cross-section multiplied by its length.
The cross-section is a triangle with base $12$ cm and perpendicular height $8$ cm — its area is half the base times height.
Evaluate the triangle’s area.
Multiply the cross-sectional area by the prism’s length ($32$ cm).

questions.stem: A swimming pool is in the shape of a rectangular prism. The pool is \(12\\text{ m}\) long, \(4\\text{ m}\) wide and \(1.5\\text{ m}\) deep. The pool is to be lined with tiles on the inside bottom and four side walls.\n\nHow many tiles are needed to line the pool if each tile is \(100\\text{ mm} \\times 100\\text{ mm}\)?
questions.hint: Calculate the surface area of the bottom and four side walls in square metres, then divide by the area of one tile in square metres.
questions.solution:
First, find the total inner surface area of the pool (bottom + 4 side walls):
- Bottom area: \(12 \times 4 = 48\text{ m}^2\)
- Front and back walls: \(2 \times (12 \times 1.5) = 36\text{ m}^2\)
- Left and right walls: \(2 \times (4 \times 1.5) = 12\text{ m}^2\)
- Total surface area: \(48 + 36 + 12 = 96\text{ m}^2\)

Convert tile dimensions to metres:
\(100\text{ mm} = 0.1\text{ m}\)
Area of one tile: \(0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01\text{ m}^2\)

Divide total area by tile area:
\[\text{Number of tiles} = 96 \div 0.01 = 9600\text{ tiles}\]

questions.stem:
A trapezoidal prism has the following dimensions for its cross-sectional front face:
- Parallel top side = \(5\\text{ cm}\), parallel bottom side = \(14\\text{ cm}\)
- Perpendicular height = \(6\\text{ cm}\), left slanted height = \(8\\text{ cm}\)
- Right slanted height = \(10\\text{ cm}\)
- The prism has a length of \(20\\text{ cm}\).

Calculate the total surface area of this solid.
questions.hint: Total Surface Area = 2 * (area of trapezoid base) + perimeter * length.
questions.solution:
Calculate front trapezoid area:
\[A_{\\text{base}} = \\frac{1}{2} \\times (5 + 14) \\times 6 = 57\\text{ cm}^2\]
Calculate perimeter of the base:
\[P = 5 + 14 + 8 + 10 = 37\\text{ cm}\]
Calculate total surface area:
\[\\text{TSA} = 2 \\times A_{\\text{base}} + P \\times L = 2 \\times 57 + 37 \\times 20 = 114 + 740 = 894\\text{ cm}^2\]

steps.explain: Calculate the area of the cross-sectional front face (a trapezoid).
Calculate the perimeter of the front face. Add up the top, bottom, and two slanted sides.
Calculate the total area of the rectangular sides wrapping around the prism.
Add the areas of the two triangular bases (front and back) to the sides area to find the Total Surface Area.

- Outer area: \(20 \\times 32 = 640\\text{ m}^2\)
- Grass area: \(640 - 288 = 352\\text{ m}^2\)

Final Answer: Subtract the inner area from the outer area. **Pitfall:** When finding the area with a border, remember that the border is added to BOTH sides (so +8, not just +4).

questions.hint: Find the side length of the square (8 cm), which is the diameter of the inscribed circle. Calculate the area of the circle (pi * 4^2) and subtract it from 64.
questions.solution:
Calculate values:
- Side length of square: \(s = \\sqrt{64} = 8\\text{ cm}\)
- Circle diameter = \(8\\text{ cm}\) (radius \(r = 4\\text{ cm}\))
- Circle area: \(A_{\\text{circle}} = \\pi \\times 4^2 = 16\\pi \\approx 50.27\\text{ cm}^2\)
- Shaded area: \(A_{\\text{shaded}} = 64 - 50.27 = 13.73\\text{ cm}^2\)
